# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

DEFUSAL MANUAL:
The light never holds. It changes every round, and it always walks the
same circle of five colours. What matters is what it shows at the
moment of the cut.

|---|---|
| orange | blue |

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

First, I take stock of who can reach whom. I am Mute: my only channel is gestures, and only Deaf can see them. Blind can neither see gestures nor hear anything I could say (I can't speak anyway), so every fact I hold must travel through Deaf — Deaf sees my gestures, sees the bomb's colours, and can speak to Blind. Deaf is the hub; I am the source. My manual says the light colour at the moment of the cut determines the wire to cut, and so far I hold exactly one row of the table: orange light → cut blue wire.

The hard problem: gestures have no shared meaning yet. I cannot literally "gesture" the word orange or blue. So this turn cannot deliver the mapping itself — it has to open the channel and start building a code with Deaf, who can answer me verbally (I can hear, I just can't speak).

My proposed seed code, chosen to be as guessable as possible: finger counts as numbers — ☝ = 1, ✌ = 2, 🤟 = 3 (three extended digits), 🤘 = 4, 🖐 = 5. I need numbers most of all, because once Deaf enumerates the wires by their physical positions aloud (which Blind can verify by touch), every future manual row can be sent as just a number: "cut position N". The five-colour circle suggests the table will keep growing one row per round, so I'll want this pipeline working before the table is complete.

So my opening to Deaf: hello, the number five (hinting at five of something — five colours in the circle, possibly five wires), a counting demo 1 through 5, then "question" (🤌, the classic *what do you want from me?*) and "call me" (🤙, *answer me*). If Deaf replies verbally — even just "five what?" or "I see five wires, red, blue..." — the channel is open and we can lock the code next round. There is no indication the bomb demands an immediate cut, and a guessed gesture could cost all three of us, so I spend this turn on protocol, not on the table.

I send nothing to Blind: they would receive only blanks and learn nothing.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🖐", "☝", "✌", "🤟", "🤘", "🖐", "🤌", "🤙"])
```

If your nine signs simply meant 'tell me what you see', just answer 👍 and consider it answered. Meanwhile here is my side: display reads 0, light is white, three wires left to right — one green, two red, three blue. Now answer me with single signs, one question at a time: does the manual rule depend on the display number? Does it depend on the light colour? Does it say to cut exactly one wire? If yes to that last one, which position — sign ☝, ✌, or 🤟. And if you meant something entirely different with those nine, sign 🤙 and I'll rethink.
Deaf gestures to Mute: [👍]

Deaf's code is now on the table and it is a good one — I adopt it exactly as proposed. Deaf answered my opening handshake with the full bomb state, so my question is already answered; no need to repeat anything.

Parsing Deaf's questions against my manual, in order: does the rule depend on the display? My manual says nothing about a display — the light is what matters. 👎. Does it depend on the light colour? Yes, explicitly: "what matters is what it shows at the moment of the cut." 👍. Does it say cut exactly one wire? Yes — the table maps a light colour to a single wire colour. 👍. Which position? My only row says cut the blue wire; Deaf reports the wires as 1 green, 2 red, 3 blue, so blue is position three — 🤟.

But the critical hold signal: the light is white right now, and white is not in my table. My only row is orange → blue. So I must sign 🖐 — nobody cuts anything this round, or we die on a guess.

Then the probe: Deaf's code only covers positions 1–3, but my manual says the light walks a circle of five colours. I will need numbers up to five, and Deaf needs to learn that "five" matters here. So I reopen my original counting demo behind the question flag 👋: one through five. Worst case Deaf reads it as "extend the number code to 4 and 5" — which I want anyway. Best case Deaf connects five to the light's cycle and starts reporting the light colour every round.

The pipeline I'm building, which I'll confirm next round once Deaf responds: Deaf reports the light colour aloud each round (I hear it, and the circle order will reveal itself across rounds); I answer each round with either 🖐 (hold — colour not in my table) or position + ✊ (cut that wire now); Deaf relays the command to Blind by voice, since I can never reach Blind directly. The one-round delivery lag is survivable only because Deaf sees the light live and can time the cut within the round — my signs carry the mapping, Deaf carries the timing.

I send nothing to Blind: gestures arrive there as blanks and would teach nothing.

That also tells Deaf the wait is bounded and that it should log each round's light colour to watch the circle emerge. No resend of my old counting string is needed; its only payload, "five," is carried by this list.

Once Deaf assigns orange a sign next round, the endgame is simple: when the light actually shows orange, Deaf verifies it live and speaks the cut order to Blind — position 3. Until then, nobody touches anything.
